First, let's simplify the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}36{x}^{2} & >49 \\ {x}^{2} & >\frac{49}{36}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use either of two methods to solve the inequality.

*Method 1 - Solving an Absolute Value Equation*

Taking the square root of both sides of the inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{x}^{2}} & >\sqrt{\frac{49}{36}} \\ |x| & >\frac{7}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the definition of absolute value, we must have 

$$
x<-\frac{7}{6}\,\text{or}\,x>\frac{7}{6}.
$$

So, the solution is $x\in (-\infty ,-\frac{7}{6})\cup (\frac{7}{6},+\infty ).$

*Method 2 - Picturing a Quadratic Curve*

Starting from ${x}^{2}>\frac{49}{36}$ and moving all terms to the left-hand side, we reach

$$
{x}^{2}-\frac{49}{36}>0.
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding parabola given by $\,y={x}^{2}-\frac{49}{36}\,$ and find its roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-\frac{49}{36} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-{(\frac{7}{6})}^{2} & =0 \\ (x-\frac{7}{6})(x+\frac{7}{6}) & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

so the roots are  $x=\pm \frac{7}{6}.$ 

Since the leading coefficient of ${x}^{2}-\frac{49}{36}$   is positive, the parabola opens upward. Hence, the solution set to the given inequality ($y>0$) lies outside the roots and does not include them:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13965374/assets/14702e7d185d38587cf10642c8a455d9d25a51d2a8eebbf7e0e54a79223ea56e.png)

 

Therefore, the solution is 

$$
x\in (-\infty ,-\frac{7}{6})\cup (\frac{7}{6},\infty ).
$$
